papers.anonymized_problem: A unified framework is studied for learning continuous control policies via backpropagation, where stochasticity in the Bellman equation is treated as a deterministic function of exogenous noise. This formulation yields a spectrum of policy gradient algorithms spanning model-free methods with value functions to model-based methods without value functions, while using learned models that require only real environment observations to limit compounded model errors. The approach is evaluated on a toy stochastic control problem and several physics-based simulated control tasks, with results demonstrating the effectiveness of simultaneously learning models, value functions, and policies in continuous domains.
papers.original_title: Learning Continuous Control Policies by Stochastic Value Gradients
papers.original_abstract: We present a unified framework for learning continuous control policies using backpropagation. It supports stochastic control by treating stochasticity in the Bellman equation as a deterministic function of exogenous noise. The product is a spectrum of general policy gradient algorithms that range from model-free methods with value functions to model-based methods without value functions. We use learned models but only require observations from the environment in- stead of observations from model-predicted trajectories, minimizing the impact of compounded model errors. We apply these algorithms first to a toy stochastic control problem and then to several physics-based control problems in simulation. One of these variants, SVG(1), shows the effectiveness of learning models, value functions, and policies simultaneously in continuous domains.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies Gaussian process models for additive functions, where the target decomposes into a sum of low-dimensional components each depending on a subset of input variables. Such a formulation generalizes both Generalized Additive Models and standard squared-exponential kernel GPs, with hyperparameter learning framed as Bayesian hierarchical kernel learning. A kernel parameterization is developed that permits tractable evaluation of all input interaction terms despite their number being exponential in the input dimension. The approach is evaluated on regression tasks, with findings indicating improved interpretability and state-of-the-art predictive performance.
papers.original_title: Additive Gaussian Processes
papers.original_abstract: We introduce a Gaussian process model of functions which are additive. An additive function is one which decomposes into a sum of low-dimensional functions, each depending on only a subset of the input variables. Additive GPs generalize both Generalized Additive Models, and the standard GP models which use squared-exponential kernels. Hyperparameter learning in this model can be seen as Bayesian Hierarchical Kernel Learning (HKL). We introduce an expressive but tractable parameterization of the kernel function, which allows efficient evaluation of all input interaction terms, whose number is exponential in the input dimension. The additional structure discoverable by this model results in increased interpretability, as well as state-of-the-art predictive power in regression tasks.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies low-rank tensor factorization in the presence of missing data, specifically examining how many sampled entries are required to efficiently and exactly reconstruct a tensor with a low-rank orthogonal decomposition. An alternating minimization approach is analyzed that iteratively refines estimates of singular vectors, with theoretical guarantees showing exact recovery of a three-mode n×n×n rank-r tensor from O(n^(3/2) r^5 log^4 n) randomly sampled entries under standard assumptions. The analysis addresses two sub-problems: initialization via a generalization of a result by Szemeredie et al. on spectra of random graphs, yielding RMSE on parameters bounded by C(r^2 n^(3/2) (log n)^4 / |Ω|) from |Ω| observations, followed by a global convergence proof for alternating minimization from that initialization. Simulations suggest the dependence of sample complexity on dimensionality n is tight.
papers.original_title: Provable Tensor Factorization with Missing Data
papers.original_abstract: We study the problem of low-rank tensor factorization in the presence of missing data. We ask the following question: how many sampled entries do we need, to efficiently and exactly reconstruct a tensor with a low-rank orthogonal decomposition? We propose a novel alternating minimization based method which iteratively refines estimates of the singular vectors. We show that under certain standard assumptions, our method can recover a three-mode n × n × n dimensional rank-r tensor exactly from O(n3/2r5 log4 n) randomly sampled entries. In the process of proving this result, we solve two challenging sub-problems for tensors with missing data. First, in analyzing the initialization step, we prove a generalization of a celebrated result by Szemeredie et al. on the spectrum of random graphs. We show that this initialization step alone is sufficient to achieve the root mean squared error on the parameters bounded by C(r2n3/2(log n)4/|Ω|) from |Ω| observed entries for some constant C independent of n and r. Next, we prove global convergence of alternating minimization with this good initialization. Simulations suggest that the dependence of the sample size on the dimensionality n is indeed tight.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies Principal Component Analysis for large tensors of arbitrary order k under a rank-one-plus-noise (single-spike) model, examining both the information-theoretic limits and the computational tractability of recovery. Information-theoretic analysis establishes that the principal component is estimable when the signal-to-noise ratio β exceeds C√(k log k), even as problem dimensions grow. Polynomial-time algorithms based on tensor unfolding, power iteration, and message passing are analyzed, with findings indicating that none succeed unless the signal-to-noise ratio diverges with system dimensions, suggesting a fundamental statistical-computational gap. The role of initialization strategies and the impact of side information on algorithmic convergence are also characterized.
papers.original_title: A statistical model for tensor PCA
papers.original_abstract:
We consider the Principal Component Analysis problem for large tensors of arbitrary order $k$ under a single-spike (or rank-one plus noise) model. On the one hand, we use information theory, and recent results in probability theory, to establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which the principal component can be estimated using unbounded computational resources. It turns out that this is possible as soon as the signal-to-noise ratio $\beta$ becomes larger than $C\sqrt{k\log k}$ (and in particular $\beta$ can remain bounded as the problem dimensions increase). 
On the other hand, we analyze several polynomial-time estimation algorithms, based on tensor unfolding, power iteration and message passing ideas from graphical models. We show that, unless the signal-to-noise ratio diverges in the system dimensions, none of these approaches succeeds. This is possibly related to a fundamental limitation of computationally tractable estimators for this problem. 
We discuss various initializations for tensor power iteration, and show that a tractable initialization based on the spectrum of the matricized tensor outperforms significantly baseline methods, statistically and computationally. Finally, we consider the case in which additional side information is available about the unknown signal. We characterize the amount of side information that allows the iterative algorithms to converge to a good estimate.

papers.anonymized_problem: Efficient exploration in reinforcement learning is typically achieved through optimism-based algorithms, but posterior sampling offers an alternative approach. A posterior sampling method for reinforcement learning is studied, in which a prior distribution over Markov decision processes is updated at the start of each episode and a single sample is drawn to determine the policy followed for that episode. A regret bound of O(τS√(AT)) is established, representing one of the first such guarantees for a non-optimism-based algorithm and competitive with the state of the art for reinforcement learning broadly. Simulation results demonstrate that the posterior sampling approach significantly outperforms existing algorithms with comparable regret bounds.
papers.original_title: (More) Efficient Reinforcement Learning via Posterior Sampling
papers.original_abstract: Most provably-efficient reinforcement learning algorithms introduce optimism about poorly-understood states and actions to encourage exploration. We study an alternative approach for efficient exploration: posterior sampling for reinforcement learning (PSRL). This algorithm proceeds in repeated episodes of known duration. At the start of each episode, PSRL updates a prior distribution over Markov decision processes and takes one sample from this posterior. PSRL then follows the policy that is optimal for this sample during the episode. The algorithm is conceptually simple, computationally efficient and allows an agent to encode prior knowledge in a natural way. We establish an O(τS/√AT) bound on expected regret, where T is time, τ is the episode length and S and A are the cardinalities of the state and action spaces. This bound is one of the first for an algorithm not based on optimism, and close to the state of the art for any reinforcement learning algorithm. We show through simulation that PSRL significantly outperforms existing algorithms with similar regret bounds.

papers.anonymized_problem: Joint density estimation of real-valued vectors is addressed through an autoregressive model that factorizes the joint density as a product of one-dimensional conditionals, each modeled using mixture density networks with shared parameters. The approach maintains a tractable likelihood expression, enabling direct comparison with baseline methods and optimization via standard gradient-based training. The model is evaluated on several datasets of heterogeneous and perceptual data, where it outperforms mixture models in all but one case.
papers.original_title: RNADE: The real-valued neural autoregressive density-estimator
papers.original_abstract: We introduce RNADE, a new model for joint density estimation of real-valued vectors. Our model calculates the density of a datapoint as the product of one-dimensional conditionals modeled using mixture density networks with shared parameters. RNADE learns a distributed representation of the data, while having a tractable expression for the calculation of densities. A tractable likelihood allows direct comparison with other methods and training by standard gradient-based optimizers. We compare the performance of RNADE on several datasets of heterogeneous and perceptual data, finding it outperforms mixture models in all but one case.

papers.anonymized_problem: Measuring nonlinear statistical dependence between random variables of arbitrary dimension is a fundamental challenge in data analysis. A coefficient is developed based on the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi Maximum Correlation Coefficient, defined in terms of correlations of random nonlinear copula projections. The approach is invariant with respect to marginal distribution transformations and is designed to have low computational cost.
papers.original_title: The Randomized Dependence Coefficient
papers.original_abstract: We introduce the Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC), a measure of nonlinear dependence between random variables of arbitrary dimension based on the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Renyi Maximum Correlation Coefficient. RDC is defined in terms of correlation of random non-linear copula projections; it is invariant with respect to marginal distribution transformations, has low computational cost and is easy to implement: just five lines of R code, included at the end of the paper.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work examines fundamental communication complexity limits for distributed convex learning and optimization, analyzing how constraints vary with the information available to individual machines and the class of functions considered. The study characterizes regimes in which existing distributed algorithms are worst-case optimal and regimes where improvement remains theoretically possible. A key finding is that without similarity among local objective functions—whether arising from statistical data homogeneity or other sources—many rounds of communication may be unavoidable even under unbounded computational resources.
papers.original_title: Communication Complexity of Distributed Convex Learning and Optimization
papers.original_abstract: We study the fundamental limits to communication-efficient distributed methods for convex learning and optimization, under different assumptions on the information available to individual machines, and the types of functions considered. We identify cases where existing algorithms are already worst-case optimal, as well as cases where room for further improvement is still possible. Among other things, our results indicate that without similarity between the local objective functions (due to statistical data similarity or otherwise) many communication rounds may be required, even if the machines have unbounded computational power.

papers.anonymized_problem: Spatio-temporal prediction of high-dimensional video frames conditioned on control variables or actions is studied in the context of vision-based reinforcement learning, specifically Atari games from the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), where scenes involve multiple interacting objects, partial observability, and dynamic object entry and departure. Two deep neural network architectures combining convolutional and recurrent components are evaluated for encoding, action-conditional transformation, and decoding of future frames. Results demonstrate that the architectures can generate visually realistic frames useful for control over approximately 100-step action-conditional futures in several games. This represents an evaluation of long-term, high-dimensional video prediction conditioned on control inputs.
papers.original_title: Action-Conditional Video Prediction using Deep Networks in Atari Games
papers.original_abstract: Motivated by vision-based reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in particular Atari games from the recent benchmark Aracade Learning Environment (ALE), we consider spatio-temporal prediction problems where future (image-)frames are dependent on control variables or actions as well as previous frames. While not composed of natural scenes, frames in Atari games are high-dimensional in size, can involve tens of objects with one or more objects being controlled by the actions directly and many other objects being influenced indirectly, can involve entry and departure of objects, and can involve deep partial observability. We propose and evaluate two deep neural network architectures that consist of encoding, action-conditional transformation, and decoding layers based on convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. Experimental results show that the proposed architectures are able to generate visually-realistic frames that are also useful for control over approximately 100-step action-conditional futures in some games. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to make and evaluate long-term predictions on high-dimensional video conditioned by control inputs.

papers.anonymized_problem: Biased Markov chain Monte Carlo procedures trade asymptotic exactness for computational speed, but standard sample quality measures such as effective sample size fail to account for asymptotic bias, complicating sampler and parameter selection. A computable quality measure based on Stein's method is developed to quantify the maximum discrepancy between sample and target expectations over a broad class of test functions. The measure is applied to compare exact, biased, and deterministic sample sequences, with demonstrated uses in hyperparameter selection, convergence rate assessment, and bias-variance tradeoff analysis in posterior inference.
papers.original_title: Measuring Sample Quality with Stein's Method
papers.original_abstract: To improve the efficiency of Monte Carlo estimation, practitioners are turning to biased Markov chain Monte Carlo procedures that trade off asymptotic exactness for computational speed. The reasoning is sound: a reduction in variance due to more rapid sampling can outweigh the bias introduced. However, the inexactness creates new challenges for sampler and parameter selection, since standard measures of sample quality like effective sample size do not account for asymptotic bias. To address these challenges, we introduce a new computable quality measure based on Stein's method that quantifies the maximum discrepancy between sample and target expectations over a large class of test functions. We use our tool to compare exact, biased, and deterministic sample sequences and illustrate applications to hyperparameter selection, convergence rate assessment, and quantifying bias-variance tradeoffs in posterior inference.

papers.anonymized_problem: Mixture models offer expressive power through weighted combination, but maximum likelihood estimation via Expectation Maximization (EM) lacks global convergence guarantees due to non-convexity. Method of moments approaches provide global guarantees for certain mixture models but do not generalize easily across the broad class of such models. A framework is developed in which mixture model moments are expressed as mixtures of polynomials of the parameters, enabling estimation to be cast as a Generalized Moment Problem solved via semidefinite optimization with parameter extraction using computer algebra techniques. Simulations demonstrate empirical performance across several models.
papers.original_title: Estimating Mixture Models via Mixtures of Polynomials
papers.original_abstract: Mixture modeling is a general technique for making any simple model more expressive through weighted combination. This generality and simplicity in part explains the success of the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm, in which updates are easy to derive for a wide class of mixture models. However, the likelihood of a mixture model is non-convex, so EM has no known global convergence guarantees. Recently, method of moments approaches offer global guarantees for some mixture models, but they do not extend easily to the range of mixture models that exist. In this work, we present Polymom, an unifying framework based on method of moments in which estimation procedures are easily derivable, just as in EM. Polymom is applicable when the moments of a single mixture component are polynomials of the parameters. Our key observation is that the moments of the mixture model are a mixture of these polynomials, which allows us to cast estimation as a Generalized Moment Problem. We solve its relaxations using semidefinite optimization, and then extract parameters using ideas from computer algebra. This framework allows us to draw insights and apply tools from convex optimization, computer algebra and the theory of moments to study problems in statistical estimation. Simulations show good empirical performance on several models.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies the problem of aggregating an ensemble of predictors with known loss bounds in a semi-supervised binary classification setting, with the goal of minimizing prediction loss on unlabeled data. Minimax optimal predictions are derived for a general class of loss functions encompassing all convex and many non-convex losses, extending prior analysis beyond misclassification error. The resulting aggregation algorithms are computationally efficient via convex optimization and achieve minimax optimality without relaxations, with decision rules that apply sigmoid functions to an ensemble margin quantity without requiring standard margin-based assumptions.
papers.original_title: Optimal Binary Classifier Aggregation for General Losses
papers.original_abstract: We address the problem of aggregating an ensemble of predictors with known loss bounds in a semi-supervised binary classification setting, to minimize prediction loss incurred on the unlabeled data. We find the minimax optimal predictions for a very general class of loss functions including all convex and many non-convex losses, extending a recent analysis of the problem for misclassification error. The result is a family of semi-supervised ensemble aggregation algorithms which are as efficient as linear learning by convex optimization, but are minimax optimal without any relaxations. Their decision rules take a form familiar in decision theory -- applying sigmoid functions to a notion of ensemble margin -- without the assumptions typically made in margin-based learning.

papers.anonymized_problem: The average-case performance of multi-task Gaussian process regression is studied through the learning curve, defined as the average Bayes error for a chosen task as a function of the total number of training examples across all tasks. For GP covariances formed as the product of an input-dependent covariance function and a free-form inter-task covariance matrix, accurate approximations to the learning curve are derived for an arbitrary number of tasks T, enabling analysis of asymptotic learning behaviour. A key finding is that multi-task learning can be asymptotically near-useless, with examples from other tasks providing benefit only when inter-task correlation is close to its maximum value, an effect most pronounced for smooth target functions such as those described by squared exponential kernels. When learning many tasks, the learning curves exhibit a two-phase structure: an initial collective-learning phase that reduces Bayes error to a plateau even for tasks with no direct observations, followed by a final decay once the number of examples is proportional to the number of tasks.
papers.original_title: Learning curves for multi-task Gaussian process regression
papers.original_abstract: We study the average case performance of multi-task Gaussian process (GP) regression as captured in the learning curve, i.e. the average Bayes error for a chosen task versus the total number of examples $n$ for all tasks. For GP covariances that are the product of an input-dependent covariance function and a free-form inter-task covariance matrix, we show that accurate approximations for the learning curve can be obtained for an arbitrary number of tasks $T$. We use these to study the asymptotic learning behaviour for large $n$. Surprisingly, multi-task learning can be asymptotically essentially useless, in the sense that examples from other tasks help only when the degree of inter-task correlation, $\rho$, is near its maximal value $\rho=1$. This effect is most extreme for learning of smooth target functions as described by e.g. squared exponential kernels. We also demonstrate that when learning many tasks, the learning curves separate into an initial phase, where the Bayes error on each task is reduced down to a plateau value by "collective learning" even though most tasks have not seen examples, and a final decay that occurs once the number of examples is proportional to the number of tasks.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies active learning for link classification in signed networks, where edge labels are generated by perturbing an initial sign assignment consistent with a two-clustering of nodes. The central question is how many edge label queries are needed to achieve near-optimal mistake bounds on general graphs. Theoretical analysis within this stochastic model shows that an optimal (to within a constant factor) number of mistakes is achievable on any graph G = (V, E) with |E| = Ω(|V|^{3/2}) by querying O(|V|^{3/2}) edge labels, and a more general algorithm achieves optimality to within a factor of O(k) by querying at most order |V| + (|V|/k)^{3/2} edge labels, with running time at most order |E| + |V| log |V|.
papers.original_title: A Linear Time Active Learning Algorithm for Link Classification
papers.original_abstract: We present very efficient active learning algorithms for link classification in signed networks. Our algorithms are motivated by a stochastic model in which edge labels are obtained through perturbations of a initial sign assignment consistent with a two-clustering of the nodes. We provide a theoretical analysis within this model, showing that we can achieve an optimal (to whithin a constant factor) number of mistakes on any graph G = (V,E) such that |E| = \Omega(|V|^{3/2}) by querying O(|V|^{3/2}) edge labels. More generally, we show an algorithm that achieves optimality to within a factor of O(k) by querying at most order of |V| + (|V|/k)^{3/2} edge labels. The running time of this algorithm is at most of order |E| + |V|\log|V|.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work investigates the conditions under which empirical risk minimization (ERM) achieves fast (1/n) versus slow (1/√n) convergence rates of excess risk in statistical learning, where data is drawn from an unknown distribution. The study examines a concept called stochastic mixability — a property of the joint triple (loss function, hypothesis class, distribution) — and establishes a direct proof that fast rates for ERM follow from this condition, leveraging a classical result by Kemperman on the general moment problem. The analysis draws a formal connection between convergence rates in statistical learning and the mixability conditions known from the prediction with expert advice setting. A partial converse result is also established, suggesting that stochastic mixability may fully characterize fast rates for ERM.
papers.original_title: From Stochastic Mixability to Fast Rates
papers.original_abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) is a fundamental learning rule for statistical learning problems where the data is generated according to some unknown distribution P and returns a hypothesis f chosen from a fixed class ℱ with small loss l. In the parametric setting, depending upon (l, ℱ, P) ERM can have slow (1/√n) or fast (1/n) rates of convergence of the excess risk as a function of the sample size n. There exist several results that give sufficient conditions for fast rates in terms of joint properties of l, ℱ, and P, such as the margin condition and the Bernstein condition. In the non-statistical prediction with expert advice setting, there is an analogous slow and fast rate phenomenon, and it is entirely characterized in terms of the mixability of the loss l (there being no role there for ℱ or P). The notion of stochastic mixability builds a bridge between these two models of learning, reducing to classical mixability in a special case. The present paper presents a direct proof of fast rates for ERM in terms of stochastic mixability of (l, ℱ, P), and in so doing provides new insight into the fast-rates phenomenon. The proof exploits an old result of Kemperman on the solution to the general moment problem. We also show a partial converse that suggests a characterization of fast rates for ERM in terms of stochastic mixability is possible.

papers.anonymized_problem: Determining whether a drug exhibits competitive or non-competitive inhibitory interaction with protein targets is a central challenge in drug design. A tensor factorization approach is studied that combines multiple measurement types (IC50 and Ki) with protein and compound data into a unified representation, using high-dimensional 2D ECFP fingerprints as side information incorporated via a noise-injection MCMC sampler to handle large-scale datasets. Using public ChEMBL data, a latent subspace separating the two measurement types is identified. Results indicate that the method can detect competitive inhibitory activity between compounds and proteins.
papers.original_title: Highly Scalable Tensor Factorization for Prediction of Drug-Protein Interaction Type
papers.original_abstract:
The understanding of the type of inhibitory interaction plays an important role in drug design. Therefore, researchers are interested to know whether a drug has competitive or non-competitive interaction to particular protein targets. 
Method: to analyze the interaction types we propose factorization method Macau which allows us to combine different measurement types into a single tensor together with proteins and compounds. The compounds are characterized by high dimensional 2D ECFP fingerprints. The novelty of the proposed method is that using a specially designed noise injection MCMC sampler it can incorporate high dimensional side information, i.e., millions of unique 2D ECFP compound features, even for large scale datasets of millions of compounds. Without the side information, in this case, the tensor factorization would be practically futile. 
Results: using public IC50 and Ki data from ChEMBL we trained a model from where we can identify the latent subspace separating the two measurement types (IC50 and Ki). The results suggest the proposed method can detect the competitive inhibitory activity between compounds and proteins.

papers.anonymized_problem: Real-time bidding (RTB) in online advertising requires clickthrough rate prediction under strict latency constraints (~100ms), making computational efficiency a core design requirement alongside predictive accuracy. The problem of representing user-website interaction as a bipartite graph and applying dimensionality reduction to produce features for clickthrough rate prediction is studied, with particular attention to the trade-off between predictive performance, feature sparsity, and runtime cost. A Bayesian nonparametric clustering approach to dimensionality reduction is evaluated against conventional schemes, with findings showing comparable predictive performance while achieving sparser feature representations and faster computation at inference time.
papers.original_title: Dimensionality reduction for click-through rate prediction: Dense versus sparse representation
papers.original_abstract: In online advertising, display ads are increasingly being placed based on real-time auctions where the advertiser who wins gets to serve the ad. This is called real-time bidding (RTB). In RTB, auctions have very tight time constraints on the order of 100ms. Therefore mechanisms for bidding intelligently such as clickthrough rate prediction need to be sufficiently fast. In this work, we propose to use dimensionality reduction of the user-website interaction graph in order to produce simplified features of users and websites that can be used as predictors of clickthrough rate. We demonstrate that the Infinite Relational Model (IRM) as a dimensionality reduction offers comparable predictive performance to conventional dimensionality reduction schemes, while achieving the most economical usage of features and fastest computations at run-time. For applications such as real-time bidding, where fast database I/O and few computations are key to success, we thus recommend using IRM based features as predictors to exploit the recommender effects from bipartite graphs.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work analyzes a multi-step stochastic variant of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) for high-dimensional optimization problems. Both the single-regularizer setting (e.g., sparse optimization) and the multi-block setting with multiple regularizers and variables (e.g., matrix decomposition into sparse and low-rank components) are studied theoretically. For sparse optimization, the method achieves the minimax rate of O(s log d/T) for s-sparse problems in d dimensions over T steps, and for matrix decomposition the analysis establishes an O(1/T) convergence rate with efficient scaling in matrix size, with minimax-optimality under independent noise models. Empirical evaluations on both problem classes demonstrate performance advantages over existing state-of-the-art methods.
papers.original_title: Multi-Step Stochastic ADMM in High Dimensions: Applications to Sparse Optimization and Matrix Decomposition
papers.original_abstract: In this paper, we consider a multi-step version of the stochastic ADMM method with efficient guarantees for high-dimensional problems. We first analyze the simple setting, where the optimization problem consists of a loss function and a single regularizer (e.g. sparse optimization), and then extend to the multi-block setting with multiple regularizers and multiple variables (e.g. matrix decomposition into sparse and low rank components). For the sparse optimization problem, our method achieves the minimax rate of O(s log d/T) for s-sparse problems in d dimensions in T steps, and is thus, unimprovable by any method up to constant factors. For the matrix decomposition problem with a general loss function, we analyze the multi-step ADMM with multiple blocks. We establish O(1/T) rate and efficient scaling as the size of matrix grows. For natural noise models (e.g. independent noise), our convergence rate is minimax-optimal. Thus, we establish tight convergence guarantees for multi-block ADMM in high dimensions. Experiments show that for both sparse optimization and matrix decomposition problems, our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

papers.anonymized_problem: Inference in general Ising models is difficult due to high treewidth making tree-based algorithms intractable, and strong interactions can cause Gibbs sampling to take exponential time to converge. An approach is examined for projecting Ising model parameters onto a parameter set guaranteed to be fast mixing under several divergences. Empirical evaluation shows that Gibbs sampling using projected parameters yields greater accuracy than using original parameters when interaction strengths are strong or when limited sampling time is available.
papers.original_title: Projecting Ising Model Parameters for Fast Mixing
papers.original_abstract: Inference in general Ising models is difficult, due to high treewidth making tree-based algorithms intractable. Moreover, when interactions are strong, Gibbs sampling may take exponential time to converge to the stationary distribution. We present an algorithm to project Ising model parameters onto a parameter set that is guaranteed to be fast mixing, under several divergences. We find that Gibbs sampling using the projected parameters is more accurate than with the original parameters when interaction strengths are strong and when limited time is available for sampling.

papers.anonymized_problem: Dimensionality reduction methods that theoretically preserve the independence structure of data modeled as samples from a union of independent subspaces have not been well studied. This work investigates how many projection vectors are sufficient to preserve subspace independence for K-class data, establishing that 2K projection vectors are sufficient for this purpose. A dimensionality reduction algorithm is developed with theoretical guarantees for preserving this union-of-subspaces structure. The approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results compared to popular dimensionality reduction techniques.
papers.original_title: Dimensionality Reduction with Subspace Structure Preservation
papers.original_abstract: Modeling data as being sampled from a union of independent subspaces has been widely applied to a number of real world applications. However, dimensionality reduction approaches that theoretically preserve this independence assumption have not been well studied. Our key contribution is to show that $2K$ projection vectors are sufficient for the independence preservation of any $K$ class data sampled from a union of independent subspaces. It is this non-trivial observation that we use for designing our dimensionality reduction technique. In this paper, we propose a novel dimensionality reduction algorithm that theoretically preserves this structure for a given dataset. We support our theoretical analysis with empirical results on both synthetic and real world data achieving \textit{state-of-the-art} results compared to popular dimensionality reduction techniques.

papers.anonymized_problem: A limitation in prevailing Few-Shot Learning (FSL) methods is examined through a causal lens: pre-trained knowledge acts as a confounder that restricts performance, as modeled via a Structural Causal Model (SCM) capturing causalities among pre-trained knowledge, sample features, and labels. Using backdoor adjustment as a causal intervention on the SCM of many-shot learning, three algorithmic implementations are derived that reframe FSL as a causal inference problem. The approach is orthogonal to existing fine-tuning and meta-learning FSL methods and can be applied on top of them. This yields state-of-the-art 1-shot and 5-shot results on miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain CUB.
papers.original_title: Interventional Few-Shot Learning
papers.original_abstract: We uncover an ever-overlooked deficiency in the prevailing Few-Shot Learning (FSL) methods: the pre-trained knowledge is indeed a confounder that limits the performance. This finding is rooted from our causal assumption: a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for the causalities among the pre-trained knowledge, sample features, and labels. Thanks to it, we propose a novel FSL paradigm: Interventional Few-Shot Learning (IFSL). Specifically, we develop three effective IFSL algorithmic implementations based on the backdoor adjustment, which is essentially a causal intervention towards the SCM of many-shot learning: the upper-bound of FSL in a causal view. It is worth noting that the contribution of IFSL is orthogonal to existing fine-tuning and meta-learning based FSL methods, hence IFSL can improve all of them, achieving a new 1-/5-shot state-of-the-art on \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and cross-domain CUB. Code is released at this https URL.

papers.anonymized_problem: Training graph neural networks (GNNs) for large-scale graphs is computationally costly, and existing pre-training approaches for GNNs lack theoretical grounding for transferability guarantees. A framework is developed that formalizes essential graph information capture as the objective of transferable GNN training, derives a rigorous transferability bound based on differences between local graph Laplacians of source and target graphs, and specifies structural requirements on node features as GNN input. Experiments on role identification and large-scale relation prediction tasks evaluate both direct-transfer and fine-tuning settings, with controlled synthetic experiments used to validate the theoretical conclusions.
papers.original_title: Transfer Learning of Graph Neural Networks with Ego-graph Information Maximization
papers.original_abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown with superior performance in various applications, but training dedicated GNNs can be costly for large-scale graphs. Some recent work started to study the pre-training of GNNs. However, none of them provide theoretical insights into the design of their frameworks, or clear requirements and guarantees towards the transferability of GNNs. In this work, we establish a theoretically grounded and practically useful framework for the transfer learning of GNNs. Firstly, we propose a novel view towards the essential graph information and advocate the capturing of it as the goal of transferable GNN training, which motivates the design of Ours, a novel GNN framework based on ego-graph information maximization to analytically achieve this goal. Secondly, we specify the requirement of structure-respecting node features as the GNN input, and derive a rigorous bound of GNN transferability based on the difference between the local graph Laplacians of the source and target graphs. Finally, we conduct controlled synthetic experiments to directly justify our theoretical conclusions. Extensive experiments on real-world networks towards role identification show consistent results in the rigorously analyzed setting of direct-transfering, while those towards large-scale relation prediction show promising results in the more generalized and practical setting of transfering with fine-tuning.

papers.anonymized_problem: Data poisoning attacks, in which an adversary manipulates a small subset of training data to control model behavior, represent a growing threat to neural networks. Prior clean-label poisoning methods have relied on hand-crafted heuristics; this work instead frames poison crafting as a bi-level optimization problem, where the inner level trains a network on poisoned data and the outer level updates the poisons to induce a target misclassification. A first-order solver for this formulation is evaluated across fine-tuning and end-to-end training scenarios, achieving misclassification of a target image 90% of the time by corrupting just 1% of the training set, and demonstrating transferability across unknown victim architectures and hyperparameters. The approach is further validated against models trained on Google Cloud AutoML Vision, establishing real-world viability.
papers.original_title: MetaPoison: Practical General-purpose Clean-label Data Poisoning
papers.original_abstract: Data poisoning--the process by which an attacker takes control of a model by making imperceptible changes to a subset of the training data--is an emerging threat in the context of neural networks. Existing attacks for data poisoning have relied on hand-crafted heuristics. Instead, we pose crafting poisons more generally as a bi-level optimization problem, where the inner level corresponds to training a network on a poisoned dataset and the outer level corresponds to updating those poisons to achieve a desired behavior on the trained model. We then propose MetaPoison, a first-order method to solve this optimization quickly. MetaPoison is effective: it outperforms previous clean-label poisoning methods by a large margin under the same setting. MetaPoison is robust: its poisons transfer to a variety of victims with unknown hyperparameters and architectures. MetaPoison is also general-purpose, working not only in fine-tuning scenarios, but also for end-to-end training from scratch with remarkable success, e.g. causing a target image to be misclassified 90% of the time via manipulating just 1% of the dataset. Additionally, MetaPoison can achieve arbitrary adversary goals not previously possible--like using poisons of one class to make a target image don the label of another arbitrarily chosen class. Finally, MetaPoison works in the real-world. We demonstrate successful data poisoning of models trained on Google Cloud AutoML Vision. Code and premade poisons are provided at this https URL

papers.anonymized_problem: The generalization gap between adaptive gradient optimizers (such as Adam) and SGD remains theoretically underexplained despite its empirical prominence. This work analyzes the local convergence behavior of both optimizer classes through the lens of heavy-tailed gradient noise, modeling the algorithms via Lévy-driven stochastic differential equations to characterize their basin-escaping dynamics. The analysis yields closed-form escaping time results showing that geometry adaptation and gradient averaging in adaptive methods increase the effective Radon measure of local basins and lighten gradient noise tails, making adaptive optimizers less likely to escape sharp minima compared to SGD. These theoretical findings, confirmed experimentally, explain why SGD tends to converge to flatter minima and consequently achieves better generalization.
papers.original_title: Towards Theoretically Understanding Why SGD Generalizes Better Than ADAM in Deep Learning
papers.original_abstract: It is not clear yet why ADAM-alike adaptive gradient algorithms suffer from worse generalization performance than SGD despite their faster training speed. This work aims to provide understandings on this generalization gap by analyzing their local convergence behaviors. Specifically, we observe the heavy tails of gradient noise in these algorithms. This motivates us to analyze these algorithms through their Levy-driven stochastic differential equations (SDEs) because of the similar convergence behaviors of an algorithm and its SDE. Then we establish the escaping time of these SDEs from a local basin. The result shows that (1) the escaping time of both SGD and ADAM~depends on the Radon measure of the basin positively and the heaviness of gradient noise negatively; (2) for the same basin, SGD enjoys smaller escaping time than ADAM, mainly because (a) the geometry adaptation in ADAM~via adaptively scaling each gradient coordinate well diminishes the anisotropic structure in gradient noise and results in larger Radon measure of a basin; (b) the exponential gradient average in ADAM~smooths its gradient and leads to lighter gradient noise tails than SGD. So SGD is more locally unstable than ADAM~at sharp minima defined as the minima whose local basins have small Radon measure, and can better escape from them to flatter ones with larger Radon measure. As flat minima here which often refer to the minima at flat or asymmetric basins/valleys often generalize better than sharp ones~\cite{keskar2016large,he2019asymmetric}, our result explains the better generalization performance of SGD over ADAM. Finally, experimental results confirm our heavy-tailed gradient noise assumption and theoretical affirmation.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies black-box adversarial attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) under the constraint that attackers have access to only a subset of nodes and can perturb only a small number of them. The approach exploits the connection between GNN backward propagation and random walks to generalize gradient-based attacks to the black-box setting, deriving an importance score analogous to PageRank for node selection. Empirical and theoretical analysis reveals a discrepancy between classification loss and mis-classification rate, where the latter exhibits a diminishing-return pattern as the number of attacked nodes grows, motivating a greedy correction procedure to account for this effect. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that this corrected selection strategy significantly increases the mis-classification rate of common GNNs without access to model parameters or predictions.
papers.original_title: Towards More Practical Adversarial Attacks on Graph Neural Networks
papers.original_abstract: We study the black-box attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) under a novel and realistic constraint: attackers have access to only a subset of nodes in the network, and they can only attack a small number of them. A node selection step is essential under this setup. We demonstrate that the structural inductive biases of GNN models can be an effective source for this type of attacks. Specifically, by exploiting the connection between the backward propagation of GNNs and random walks, we show that the common gradient-based white-box attacks can be generalized to the black-box setting via the connection between the gradient and an importance score similar to PageRank. In practice, we find attacks based on this importance score indeed increase the classification loss by a large margin, but they fail to significantly increase the mis-classification rate. Our theoretical and empirical analyses suggest that there is a discrepancy between the loss and mis-classification rate, as the latter presents a diminishing-return pattern when the number of attacked nodes increases. Therefore, we propose a greedy procedure to correct the importance score that takes into account of the diminishing-return pattern. Experimental results show that the proposed procedure can significantly increase the mis-classification rate of common GNNs on real-world data without access to model parameters nor predictions.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work analyzes two distributed optimization strategies—Minibatch SGD and Local SGD (also known as parallel or federated SGD)—in the heterogeneous setting where each machine holds stochastic gradient estimates for a distinct convex objective and communication between machines is intermittent. The study finds that Minibatch SGD (even without acceleration) dominates all prior analyses of Local SGD in this regime, and that accelerated Minibatch SGD is optimal under high heterogeneity. An upper bound for Local SGD is also established that improves over Minibatch SGD in certain non-homogeneous regimes.
papers.original_title: Minibatch vs Local SGD for Heterogeneous Distributed Learning
papers.original_abstract: We analyze Local SGD (aka parallel or federated SGD) and Minibatch SGD in the heterogeneous distributed setting, where each machine has access to stochastic gradient estimates for a different, machine-specific, convex objective; the goal is to optimize w.r.t. the average objective; and machines can only communicate intermittently. We argue that, (i) Minibatch SGD (even without acceleration) dominates all existing analysis of Local SGD in this setting, (ii) accelerated Minibatch SGD is optimal when the heterogeneity is high, and (iii) present the first upper bound for Local SGD that improves over Minibatch SGD in a non-homogeneous regime.

papers.anonymized_problem: Self-distillation — the process of retraining a model using its own predictions as targets — empirically improves held-out accuracy, yet the theoretical mechanism behind this gain has remained unexplained. This work provides a theoretical analysis of self-distillation in the setting of nonlinear function fitting with L2 regularization in Hilbert space, showing that successive self-distillation iterations progressively constrain the number of basis functions available to represent the solution, effectively amplifying regularization. This framing explains why early rounds of self-distillation can reduce overfitting while additional rounds risk underfitting and performance degradation, a pattern confirmed empirically.
papers.original_title: Self-Distillation Amplifies Regularization in Hilbert Space
papers.original_abstract: Knowledge distillation introduced in the deep learning context is a method to transfer knowledge from one architecture to another. In particular, when the architectures are identical, this is called self-distillation. The idea is to feed in predictions of the trained model as new target values for retraining (and iterate this loop possibly a few times). It has been empirically observed that the self-distilled model often achieves higher accuracy on held out data. Why this happens, however, has been a mystery: the self-distillation dynamics does not receive any new information about the task and solely evolves by looping over training. To the best of our knowledge, there is no rigorous understanding of why this happens. This work provides the first theoretical analysis of self-distillation. We focus on fitting a nonlinear function to training data, where the model space is Hilbert space and fitting is subject to L2 regularization in this function space. We show that self-distillation iterations modify regularization by progressively limiting the number of basis functions that can be used to represent the solution. This implies (as we also verify empirically) that while a few rounds of self-distillation may reduce over-fitting, further rounds may lead to under-fitting and thus worse performance.

papers.anonymized_problem: Patch adversarial attacks, where an attacker distorts pixels within a bounded region, pose a significant threat model for physical adversarial attacks, yet certifiable defenses against them remain limited. A certifiable defense approach based on a de-randomized variant of randomized smoothing is studied, exploiting the constrained structure of patch attacks to derive deterministic robustness certificates without expensive adversarial training. The sole prior certifiable method, based on interval bound propagation, struggles to scale beyond MNIST and performs poorly on CIFAR-10, whereas the studied approach achieves approximately 57.8% certified accuracy on CIFAR-10 for a 5×5 patch attack (with 83.9% clean accuracy), compared to at most 30.3% certified accuracy for the prior method, and additionally scales to ImageNet.
papers.original_title: (De)Randomized Smoothing for Certifiable Defense against Patch Attacks
papers.original_abstract: Patch adversarial attacks on images, in which the attacker can distort pixels within a region of bounded size, are an important threat model since they provide a quantitative model for physical adversarial attacks. In this paper, we introduce a certifiable defense against patch attacks that guarantees for a given image and patch attack size, no patch adversarial examples exist. Our method is related to the broad class of randomized smoothing robustness schemes which provide high-confidence probabilistic robustness certificates. By exploiting the fact that patch attacks are more constrained than general sparse attacks, we derive meaningfully large robustness certificates. Additionally, the algorithm we propose is de-randomized, providing deterministic certificates. To the best of our knowledge, there exists only one prior method for certifiable defense against patch attacks, which relies on interval bound propagation. While this sole existing method performs well on MNIST, it has several limitations: it requires computationally expensive training, does not scale to ImageNet, and performs poorly on CIFAR-10. In contrast, our proposed method effectively addresses all of these issues: our classifier can be trained quickly, achieves high clean and certified robust accuracy on CIFAR-10, and provides certificates at the ImageNet scale. For example, for a 5*5 patch attack on CIFAR-10, our method achieves up to around 57.8% certified accuracy (with a classifier around 83.9% clean accuracy), compared to at most 30.3% certified accuracy for the existing method (with a classifier with around 47.8% clean accuracy), effectively establishing a new state-of-the-art. Code is available at this https URL.

papers.anonymized_problem: Identifying sparse trainable subnetworks at initialization—without access to training data—is studied through the lens of a mathematically formulated conservation law governing synaptic strengths. Existing gradient-based pruning-at-initialization methods are shown, both theoretically and experimentally, to suffer from layer-collapse (the premature removal of entire layers that renders a network untrainable), and the conservation law is used to derive conditions under which layer-collapse is provably avoided. A data-agnostic pruning algorithm based on preserving total synaptic flow through the network under a sparsity constraint is developed and evaluated. The approach consistently matches or surpasses prior pruning-at-initialization methods across VGG and ResNet architectures, CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet datasets, and sparsity levels up to 99.99 percent, challenging the assumption that training data is necessary to identify important synapses at initialization.
papers.original_title: Pruning neural networks without any data by iteratively conserving synaptic flow
papers.original_abstract: Pruning the parameters of deep neural networks has generated intense interest due to potential savings in time, memory and energy both during training and at test time. Recent works have identified, through an expensive sequence of training and pruning cycles, the existence of winning lottery tickets or sparse trainable subnetworks at initialization. This raises a foundational question: can we identify highly sparse trainable subnetworks at initialization, without ever training, or indeed without ever looking at the data? We provide an affirmative answer to this question through theory driven algorithm design. We first mathematically formulate and experimentally verify a conservation law that explains why existing gradient-based pruning algorithms at initialization suffer from layer-collapse, the premature pruning of an entire layer rendering a network untrainable. This theory also elucidates how layer-collapse can be entirely avoided, motivating a novel pruning algorithm Iterative Synaptic Flow Pruning (SynFlow). This algorithm can be interpreted as preserving the total flow of synaptic strengths through the network at initialization subject to a sparsity constraint. Notably, this algorithm makes no reference to the training data and consistently competes with or outperforms existing state-of-the-art pruning algorithms at initialization over a range of models (VGG and ResNet), datasets (CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet), and sparsity constraints (up to 99.99 percent). Thus our data-agnostic pruning algorithm challenges the existing paradigm that, at initialization, data must be used to quantify which synapses are important.

papers.anonymized_problem: Neural network models trained on naturalistic tasks encounter input features that vary in their relevance and predictive utility, yet the principles governing which features are represented or suppressed remain poorly understood. Using synthetic datasets with controlled feature relevance, this work investigates how models select among redundant or competing features, finding that linear decodability in untrained models predicts feature preference, that easier weakly-predictive features can suppress harder strongly-predictive ones, and that training enhances task-relevant while partially suppressing task-irrelevant features. Models trained on both easy and hard features develop representations most similar to those trained on easy features alone, and easy features yield more consistent representations across runs than hard features. These findings characterize the complex dynamics by which feature representations are shaped during learning.
papers.original_title: What shapes feature representations? Exploring datasets, architectures, and training
papers.original_abstract: In naturalistic learning problems, a model's input contains a wide range of features, some useful for the task at hand, and others not. Of the useful features, which ones does the model use? Of the task-irrelevant features, which ones does the model represent? Answers to these questions are important for understanding the basis of models' decisions, as well as for building models that learn versatile, adaptable representations useful beyond the original training task. We study these questions using synthetic datasets in which the task-relevance of input features can be controlled directly. We find that when two features redundantly predict the labels, the model preferentially represents one, and its preference reflects what was most linearly decodable from the untrained model. Over training, task-relevant features are enhanced, and task-irrelevant features are partially suppressed. Interestingly, in some cases, an easier, weakly predictive feature can suppress a more strongly predictive, but more difficult one. Additionally, models trained to recognize both easy and hard features learn representations most similar to models that use only the easy feature. Further, easy features lead to more consistent representations across model runs than do hard features. Finally, models have greater representational similarity to an untrained model than to models trained on a different task. Our results highlight the complex processes that determine which features a model represents.

papers.anonymized_problem: Autoregressive spike train models trained via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) for one-step prediction often generate poor multi-step samples, failing to capture key data features and exhibiting diverging firing rates. An alternative training objective is studied that directly minimizes the divergence between recorded and model-generated spike trains using spike train kernels, with stochastic optimization of the maximum mean discrepancy induced by the kernel. Experiments on real and synthetic neural data show this approach produces well-behaved generative models and allows control over the trade-off between different spike train features, which is important for handling model-mismatch.
papers.original_title: Rescuing neural spike train models from bad MLE
papers.original_abstract: The standard approach to fitting an autoregressive spike train model is to maximize the likelihood for one-step prediction. This maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) often leads to models that perform poorly when generating samples recursively for more than one time step. Moreover, the generated spike trains can fail to capture important features of the data and even show diverging firing rates. To alleviate this, we propose to directly minimize the divergence between neural recorded and model generated spike trains using spike train kernels. We develop a method that stochastically optimizes the maximum mean discrepancy induced by the kernel. Experiments performed on both real and synthetic neural data validate the proposed approach, showing that it leads to well-behaving models. Using different combinations of spike train kernels, we show that we can control the trade-off between different features which is critical for dealing with model-mismatch.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies bandit convex optimization in a comparator-adaptive setting, a regime previously examined only for full-information counterparts. Algorithms are developed for both linear bandits and convex bandits with Lipschitz or smooth loss functions, targeting regret bounds that scale favorably when the comparator norm is small. The approach adapts full-information techniques to the bandit setting and introduces a single-point gradient estimator alongside carefully designed surrogate losses.
papers.original_title: Comparator-adaptive Convex Bandits
papers.original_abstract: We study bandit convex optimization methods that adapt to the norm of the comparator, a topic that has only been studied before for its full-information counterpart. Specifically, we develop convex bandit algorithms with regret bounds that are small whenever the norm of the comparator is small. We first use techniques from the full-information setting to develop comparator-adaptive algorithms for linear bandits. Then, we extend the ideas to convex bandits with Lipschitz or smooth loss functions, using a new single-point gradient estimator and carefully designed surrogate losses.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work studies the theoretical limits of online recommendation systems where m users are sequentially served items from a catalogue of n items, with the constraint that no item may be recommended twice to the same user and item-user preference probabilities are unknown. The problem is analyzed under various structural assumptions on preference probabilities, with performance measured via regret relative to an oracle with full knowledge of those probabilities. Regret lower bounds are derived for each structural setting, and matching algorithms are constructed. The analysis decomposes regret into distinct components: one attributable to the no-repeat constraint, one to learning preference probabilities, and one to learning the underlying structure.
papers.original_title: Regret in Online Recommendation Systems
papers.original_abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical analysis of recommendation systems in an online setting, where items are sequentially recommended to users over time. In each round, a user, randomly picked from a population of $m$ users, requests a recommendation. The decision-maker observes the user and selects an item from a catalogue of $n$ items. Importantly, an item cannot be recommended twice to the same user. The probabilities that a user likes each item are unknown. The performance of the recommendation algorithm is captured through its regret, considering as a reference an Oracle algorithm aware of these probabilities. We investigate various structural assumptions on these probabilities: we derive for each structure regret lower bounds, and devise algorithms achieving these limits. Interestingly, our analysis reveals the relative weights of the different components of regret: the component due to the constraint of not presenting the same item twice to the same user, that due to learning the chances users like items, and finally that arising when learning the underlying structure.

papers.anonymized_problem: Neural networks frequently rely on computationally expensive matrix operations such as matrix inversion, many of which can be accelerated when the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is available. Prior methods enable the use of SVD within neural networks without explicitly computing it, but have not achieved practical speed improvements in practice. An algorithm is studied that increases the degree of parallelism in matrix multiplications of the form H·X, where H is an orthogonal matrix represented as a product of Householder matrices, yielding real-world speedups for several matrix operations. The approach bridges the gap between theoretical and practical performance of SVD-based techniques in neural network computation.
papers.original_title: What if Neural Networks had SVDs?
papers.original_abstract: Various Neural Networks employ time-consuming matrix operations like matrix inversion. Many such matrix operations are faster to compute given the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Previous work allows using the SVD in Neural Networks without computing it. In theory, the techniques can speed up matrix operations, however, in practice, they are not fast enough. We present an algorithm that is fast enough to speed up several matrix operations. The algorithm increases the degree of parallelism of an underlying matrix multiplication $H\cdot X$ where $H$ is an orthogonal matrix represented by a product of Householder matrices. Code is available at this http URL .

papers.anonymized_problem: Stationary kernels struggle to adapt to functions whose smoothness varies across inputs, limiting their expressiveness in nonstationary settings. This work investigates an approach that warps inputs as conditional Gaussian measures to control the smoothness of a stationary kernel, enabling the capture of nonstationary patterns with intuitive inductive bias. The resulting framework relies on sparse spectrum Gaussian processes to admit closed-form solutions and supports stacked constructions for modeling more complex patterns. The approach is validated on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating strong parameter efficiency across both small and large data regimes.
papers.original_title: Sparse Spectrum Warped Input Measures for Nonstationary Kernel Learning
papers.original_abstract: We establish a general form of explicit, input-dependent, measure-valued warpings for learning nonstationary kernels. While stationary kernels are ubiquitous and simple to use, they struggle to adapt to functions that vary in smoothness with respect to the input. The proposed learning algorithm warps inputs as conditional Gaussian measures that control the smoothness of a standard stationary kernel. This construction allows us to capture non-stationary patterns in the data and provides intuitive inductive bias. The resulting method is based on sparse spectrum Gaussian processes, enabling closed-form solutions, and is extensible to a stacked construction to capture more complex patterns. The method is extensively validated alongside related algorithms on synthetic and real world datasets. We demonstrate a remarkable efficiency in the number of parameters of the warping functions in learning problems with both small and large data regimes.

papers.anonymized_problem: Existing inductive unsupervised graph representation methods learn node and edge representations by predicting observed edges, making them ineffective at jointly representing larger k-node sets (k > 2). This work investigates combining joint k-node representations with energy-based models (hypergraph Markov networks) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for inductive unsupervised learning. To address the intractability of the resulting loss, an optimization approach using a finite-sample unbiased Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimator as a loss upper bound is employed. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting unsupervised representations outperform existing approaches from the literature.
papers.original_title: Unsupervised Joint k-node Graph Representations with Compositional Energy-Based Models
papers.original_abstract: Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN) methods that learn inductive unsupervised graph representations focus on learning node and edge representations by predicting observed edges in the graph. Although such approaches have shown advances in downstream node classification tasks, they are ineffective in jointly representing larger $k$-node sets, $k{>}2$. We propose MHM-GNN, an inductive unsupervised graph representation approach that combines joint $k$-node representations with energy-based models (hypergraph Markov networks) and GNNs. To address the intractability of the loss that arises from this combination, we endow our optimization with a loss upper bound using a finite-sample unbiased Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimator. Our experiments show that the unsupervised MHM-GNN representations of MHM-GNN produce better unsupervised representations than existing approaches from the literature.

papers.anonymized_problem: Boolean Tensor Decomposition (BTD) — factorizing a binary tensor into the Boolean sum of multiple rank-1 tensors — is an NP-hard problem, and existing methods are limited by high computational cost when applied to large-scale or higher-order tensors. A computationally efficient algorithm is studied that sequentially identifies rank-1 basis components from a geometric perspective, with theoretical analysis of its validity and algorithmic efficiency for all-order tensors. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improvements in reconstruction accuracy and latent structure extraction, with runtime an order of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.original_title: Geometric All-Way Boolean Tensor Decomposition
papers.original_abstract: Boolean tensor has been broadly utilized in representing high dimensional logical data collected on spatial, temporal and/or other relational domains. Boolean Tensor Decomposition (BTD) factorizes a binary tensor into the Boolean sum of multiple rank-1 tensors, which is an NP-hard problem. Existing BTD methods have been limited by their high computational cost, in applications to large scale or higher order tensors. In this work, we presented a computationally efficient BTD algorithm, namely \textit{Geometric Expansion for all-order Tensor Factorization} (GETF), that sequentially identifies the rank-1 basis components for a tensor from a geometric perspective. We conducted rigorous theoretical analysis on the validity as well as algorithemic efficiency of GETF in decomposing all-order tensor. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrated that GETF has significantly improved performance in reconstruction accuracy, extraction of latent structures and it is an order of magnitude faster than other state-of-the-art methods.

papers.anonymized_problem: The Thermodynamic Variational Objective (TVO), a variational lower bound on the log evidence based on a one-dimensional Riemann integral approximation, requires selecting a sorted schedule of discretization points whose quality directly affects model learning and inference. A Gaussian process bandit optimization approach is studied as a mechanism for automatically selecting and dynamically adapting these integration points throughout optimization. Theoretical guarantees are provided showing convergence to the regret-minimizing choice of integration points. Empirical results demonstrate improved learning and inference in Variational Autoencoders and Sigmoid Belief Networks.
papers.original_title: Gaussian Process Bandit Optimization of theThermodynamic Variational Objective
papers.original_abstract: Achieving the full promise of the Thermodynamic Variational Objective (TVO), a recently proposed variational lower bound on the log evidence involving a one-dimensional Riemann integral approximation, requires choosing a "schedule" of sorted discretization points. This paper introduces a bespoke Gaussian process bandit optimization method for automatically choosing these points. Our approach not only automates their one-time selection, but also dynamically adapts their positions over the course of optimization, leading to improved model learning and inference. We provide theoretical guarantees that our bandit optimization converges to the regret-minimizing choice of integration points. Empirical validation of our algorithm is provided in terms of improved learning and inference in Variational Autoencoders and Sigmoid Belief Networks.

papers.anonymized_problem: This work analytically characterizes the role of active sub-networks in deep neural networks with ReLU activations, where the on/off gating behavior of ReLU units determines which subset of weights contributes to any given prediction. The gate activation states and network weights are encoded into two structured representations whose inner product exactly recovers the network output, and an associated kernel over gate activation patterns is identified as a fundamental quantity characterizing information stored in the network's gates. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that these gate-derived representations are learned during training and that such learning is critical for generalization, including when the two representations are trained in separate networks.
papers.original_title: Neural Path Features and Neural Path Kernel : Understanding the role of gates in deep learning
papers.original_abstract: Rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations can also be thought of as \emph{gates}, which, either pass or stop their pre-activation input when they are \emph{on} (when the pre-activation input is positive) or \emph{off} (when the pre-activation input is negative) respectively. A deep neural network (DNN) with ReLU activations has many gates, and the {on/off} status of each gate changes across input examples as well as network weights. For a given input example, only a subset of gates are \emph{active}, i.e., on, and the sub-network of weights connected to these active gates is responsible for producing the output. At randomised initialisation, the active sub-network corresponding to a given input example is random. During training, as the weights are learnt, the active sub-networks are also learnt, and potentially hold very valuable information. In this paper, we analytically characterise the role of active sub-networks in deep learning. To this end, we encode the {on/off} state of the gates of a given input in a novel \emph{neural path feature} (NPF), and the weights of the DNN are encoded in a novel \emph{neural path value} (NPV). Further, we show that the output of network is indeed the inner product of NPF and NPV. The main result of the paper shows that the \emph{neural path kernel} associated with the NPF is a fundamental quantity that characterises the information stored in the gates of a DNN. We show via experiments (on MNIST and CIFAR-10) that in standard DNNs with ReLU activations NPFs are learnt during training and such learning is key for generalisation. Furthermore, NPFs and NPVs can be learnt in two separate networks and such learning also generalises well in experiments.

papers.anonymized_problem: Convolutional neural networks trained on large labeled datasets have driven advances in image classification and object detection, but it remains unclear whether their learned features support fine-grained spatial correspondence beyond coarse category-level recognition. This work investigates the effectiveness of convnet activation features for correspondence-dependent tasks, examining whether such features localize at scales finer than their receptive fields and whether they support intraclass alignment. Experiments on keypoint prediction using PASCAL VOC 2011 provide evidence that convnet features outperform conventional hand-engineered features on these fine-grained localization tasks.
papers.original_title: Do Convnets Learn Correspondence?
papers.original_abstract: Convolutional neural nets (convnets) trained from massive labeled datasets [1] have substantially improved the state-of-the-art in image classification [2] and object detection [3]. However, visual understanding requires establishing correspondence on a finer level than object category. Given their large pooling regions and training from whole-image labels, it is not clear that convnets derive their success from an accurate correspondence model which could be used for precise localization. In this paper, we study the effectiveness of convnet activation features for tasks requiring correspondence. We present evidence that convnet features localize at a much finer scale than their receptive field sizes, that they can be used to perform intraclass aligment as well as conventional hand-engineered features, and that they outperform conventional features in keypoint prediction on objects from PASCAL VOC 2011 [4].

papers.anonymized_problem: Gaussian Process (GP) models trained via Type-II maximum likelihood (ML-II) produce point estimates of kernel hyperparameters, which risks underestimating predictive uncertainty, overfitting in high-dimensional hyperparameter spaces, and susceptibility to local minima during gradient-based optimization. An alternative learning procedure is examined in which kernel hyperparameters are marginalized using Nested Sampling (NS), a technique suited to complex, multi-modal distributions, applied to regression tasks with spectral mixture (SM) kernels. This approach is evaluated across synthetic and benchmark datasets, with findings showing substantial gains in predictive performance compared to ML-II. Nested Sampling is also found to offer a speed advantage over Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) in this setting.
papers.original_title: Marginalised Gaussian Processes with Nested Sampling
papers.original_abstract: Gaussian Process (GPs) models are a rich distribution over functions with inductive biases controlled by a kernel function. Learning occurs through the optimisation of kernel hyperparameters using the marginal likelihood as the objective. This classical approach known as Type-II maximum likelihood (ML-II) yields point estimates of the hyperparameters, and continues to be the default method for training GPs. However, this approach risks underestimating predictive uncertainty and is prone to overfitting especially when there are many hyperparameters. Furthermore, gradient based optimisation makes ML-II point estimates highly susceptible to the presence of local minima. This work presents an alternative learning procedure where the hyperparameters of the kernel function are marginalised using Nested Sampling (NS), a technique that is well suited to sample from complex, multi-modal distributions.
